title: Two Mussar schools
hook: Novarodok taught fierce self-scrutiny; Slabodka taught human greatness

segments.voice: Yesterday's line was holiness is given: effort first, then open hands. Did you take your one step and leave the rest? Today, two very different ways of doing the work. Day one thousand two hundred eighty-three.

Two coaches watch the same young runner stumble. The first walks over and says: let's look hard at what went wrong, every step of it, and not flinch. The second walks over and says: do you have any idea what you're capable of? Both want the runner to get better. Both love the sport. They just start from opposite ends. The Mussar movement, the one Rabbi Israel Salanter began, grew into schools like that, each with its own yeshiva and its own temperament. Today, two of them, standing side by side.
screen: `TWO COACHES, ONE RUNNER.` → `LOOK HARD, OR LOOK UP.` → `TWO SCHOOLS OF MUSSAR.`

segments.voice: Turn the two schools four ways. First, Novarodok. Its founder was Rabbi Yosef Yozel Horowitz, remembered as the Alter, the elder, of Novarodok. His school taught fierce self-scrutiny: a person should look straight at their own motives, especially the hidden wish to be admired, and not look away. Second, how fierce. Stories are told of Novarodok students sent into a shop to ask, out loud, for something the shop plainly didn't sell. The point, as the stories tell it, was to stand there while people laughed, and learn that their opinion did not have to run your life. Whether every story happened just that way, nobody can promise. The aim behind them is clear: freedom from the crowd. Third, Slabodka. Its leader was Rabbi Nosson Tzvi Finkel, also called the Alter, of Slabodka. His school started from the other end, with a phrase that became its banner: gadlut ha-adam, the greatness of the human being. The root is in Genesis: "And God created man in His own image, in the image of God created He him." Slabodka students were taught to see that image in themselves and in everyone, and to dress, speak and carry themselves with the dignity it deserves. Fourth, the shared ground. Both schools came out of the same movement and asked the same question: how does a person actually change? Novarodok said: see your smallness honestly. Slabodka said: see your greatness, and you won't want to act small. Some students of Mussar start from one door, some from the other, and some walk through both.
screen: `NOVARODOK: LOOK STRAIGHT AT YOURSELF.` · `FREE FROM THE CROWD.` · `SLABODKA: THE GREATNESS OF THE HUMAN.` · `ONE QUESTION, TWO DOORS.` · then, large: `HUMAN GREATNESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: see one greatness in yourself. It may feel odd. Sit, and breathe. Let one true, good thing about you come to mind. Not a trophy; something quieter. The way you show up for a friend. A patience you didn't use to have. A stubborn honesty. Name it plainly, without a joke to soften it. Then ask Slabodka's question: if that greatness is real, what is beneath it? What small thing would you stop doing today because it doesn't fit who you are? If you pray, you can give thanks for it in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Two Mussar schools: Novarodok, with its fierce self-scrutiny, and Slabodka, with gadlut ha-adam, the greatness of the human being. Today's word.
Your line: human greatness. Today, catch one moment when you're about to act small, and act like the person you named in the quiet. Day one thousand two hundred eighty-three.

howItsDone: Mussar study today draws on both schools: some groups emphasize a hard, honest look at one's motives, others begin from the dignity of every person created in God's image, and many teachers mix the two.

trapdoor: what you thought: Mussar is all about feeling bad about yourself.
what it means: Mussar schools differed: Novarodok looked hard at a person's smallness, Slabodka at a person's greatness.
what a scholar hears: Slabodka's gadlut ha-adam rests on Genesis 1:27, the human made in the image of God.
